title: Students for Fair Admissions, Inc. v. President and Fellows of Harvard College (2023)
shortTitle: Students for Fair Admissions, Inc. v. President and Fellows of Harvard College — standing note
summary: A voluntary membership organization that identifies its members and represents them in good faith satisfies the Hunt requirements for organizational standing without further inquiry into member control and funding.
notes:
Key line: "Where, as here, an organization has identified members and represents them in good faith, our cases do not require further scrutiny into how the organization operates." Chief Justice Roberts, for the Court.

Citation: 600 U.S. 181 (2023).

sections.Parties: Petitioner was Students for Fair Admissions, Inc. (SFFA), a nonprofit organization founded in 2014 whose stated purpose is to defend human and civil rights secured by law, including the right of individuals to equal protection. Respondents were the President and Fellows of Harvard College and, in the companion case, the University of North Carolina and its officials. SFFA sued on behalf of its members, who included applicants denied admission to the two universities. The universities argued that SFFA was not a genuine membership organization when it filed suit because its members did not control or fund it.
sections.Material Facts: SFFA filed suit against Harvard and UNC in November 2014, alleging that their race-conscious admissions programs violated Title VI of the Civil Rights Act and, as to UNC, the Equal Protection Clause. When it filed, SFFA was a validly incorporated 501(c)(3) nonprofit with 47 members who had joined voluntarily to support its mission. In the UNC case SFFA identified four members in particular, high school graduates denied admission to UNC, who filed declarations stating that they had voluntarily joined SFFA, supported its mission, received updates from its president and had the opportunity to give input and direction on the case. Harvard's admissions process used race as a determinative tip for a significant percentage of admitted African American and Hispanic applicants, and UNC readers were required to consider race as one factor.
sections.Procedural History: In the Harvard case the District Court for the District of Massachusetts held after a bench trial in 2019 that SFFA had standing and that Harvard's program was lawful, and the First Circuit affirmed in 2020. In the UNC case the District Court for the Middle District of North Carolina rejected the standing challenge in 2018 and upheld UNC's program after a 2021 trial. The Supreme Court granted certiorari in both cases and certiorari before judgment in the UNC case, heard argument on October 31, 2022, and on June 29, 2023 reversed both judgments.
sections.Issue: An organization may sue on behalf of its members under Hunt when the members would have standing, the interests at stake are germane to its purpose, and individual participation is unnecessary. Harvard and UNC argued that Hunt also requires a genuine membership organization, meaning one controlled and funded by its members, and that SFFA did not qualify when it filed suit because its members did not then control or finance it. Does SFFA, a voluntary membership organization with identified members who were denied admission, have Article III standing under Hunt to challenge the universities' admissions programs on behalf of those members?
sections.Holding: Yes. Hunt's indicia of membership analysis applies only to entities like state agencies that have no members at all. SFFA is a voluntary membership organization with identifiable members who joined to support its mission, including applicants denied admission who filed declarations. Where an organization has identified members and represents them in good faith, the Court's cases do not require further scrutiny into how the organization operates. SFFA satisfied Article III.
sections.Reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts explained that an organization may sue on behalf of its members when its members would have standing in their own right, the interests at stake are germane to its purpose, and neither the claim nor the relief requires individual participation. The universities did not dispute those elements but argued that SFFA was not a genuine membership organization under Hunt. The Court read Hunt differently. Hunt involved the Washington State Apple Advertising Commission, a state agency with no members; the Court there asked whether the apple growers and dealers who elected, served on and financed the Commission possessed the indicia of membership so that the Commission was a membership organization in substance. That inquiry has no application to a group that is indisputably a voluntary membership organization with identifiable members. SFFA was such a group at the time of filing, with 47 members, and in the UNC litigation four identified members had been denied admission and had declared their voluntary participation and support. The Court concluded that SFFA complied with the requirements demanded of organizational plaintiffs and that its Article III obligations were satisfied. The Court went on to hold on the merits that both admissions programs violated the Equal Protection Clause.

topics.lrs-n-standing-association: The note distinguishes a genuine voluntary membership organization from Hunt’s state-agency setting.

learning.separateOpinions: The vote was 6 to 3 in the UNC case and 6 to 2 in the Harvard case, from which Justice Jackson was recused. Justices Thomas, Gorsuch and Kavanaugh each filed concurrences on the merits. Justice Sotomayor dissented, joined by Justice Kagan and, in the UNC case, Justice Jackson; Justice Jackson also filed a dissent in the UNC case. None of the separate opinions disputed the standing holding.
